BLM Tres Rios Field Office: Dawson project area UAS data George Woolsey 28 July, 2026 Section 1 Introduction The Dawson vegetation treatment project area is located near Dolores, Colorado (USA) on land managed by the BLM Southwest District, Tres Rios Field Office (TRFO). On April 29th and 30th, 2025, BLM Remote Sensing staff mapped approximately 2,000 acres of the Dawson site using an Uncrewed Aerial System (UAS). In total 24 flights were conducted to collect ~5,500 stereo-images. The raw imagery was then processed photogrammetrically with Agisoft Metashape software to produce high-resolution geospatial data products including 3D point cloud data and an RGB spectral orthomosaic. 1.1 Objective The objective of this analysis is to process the aerial point cloud data using the cloud2trees framework (Woolsey et al. 2025) for generating individual tree forest inventory data. cloud2trees provides a streamlined, open-source framework for generating broad-area individual tree inventories from aerial point cloud data. The primary outputs are spatial datasets of tree locations and crown polygons attributed with biophysical metrics such as height, crown dimensions, crown base height (CBH), diameter at breast height (DBH), and crown biomass. While height and location are inherently determined through the detection process, the framework augments these inventories with tree-level biophysical information determined via allometric estimates and integrated supplementary data. These high-resolution datasets support a wide range of applications including fire behavior modeling, evaluation of forest management activities, and habitat characterization.

Section 2 Point Cloud Processing In this section we’ll process the raw point cloud data using cloud2trees developed to provide accessible routines for processing point cloud data collected by airborne lidar or generated using UAS imagery and photogrammetry (e.g. structure from motion). The cloud2trees package can be installed by following the directions listed in the README file on GitHub. If one is still experiencing difficulties installing the package, see the example.R file which details how to install the package using a virgin R instance. ### ```{r,eval=T ## remotes helps us get packages hosted on github install.packages("remotes") ## get cloud2trees remotes::install_github(repo = "georgewoolsey/cloud2trees", upgrade = F) Load the standard libraries we use to do work # bread-and-butter library(tidyverse) # the tidyverse library(viridis) # viridis colors library(harrypotter) # hp colors library(RColorBrewer) # brewer colors library(scales) # work with number and plot scales library(latex2exp) # visualization library(mapview) # interactive html maps library(kableExtra) # tables library(patchwork) # combine plots library(ggnewscale) # ggnewscale library(cowplot) # cowplot # spatial analysis library(terra) # raster library(sf) # simple features library(lidR) # lidar data library(cloud2trees) # the cloud2trees 2.1 Data Location Let’s check out the location of the data we got # directory with the downloaded .las|.laz files f <- "d:/BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment/Final/PointCloud/Tiles" # f <- "d:/BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment/Final/PointCloud/Full/" # is there data? list.files(f, pattern = ".*\\.(laz|las)$") %>% length() ## [1] 187 # what files are in here? list.files(f, pattern = ".*\\.(laz|las)$")[1:3] ## [1] "BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment_PointCloud_202504-0-0.laz" ## [2] "BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment_PointCloud_202504-0-1.laz" ## [3] "BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment_PointCloud_202504-0-10.laz" what information does lidR read from the catalog? ctg_temp <- lidR::readLAScatalog(f) ctg_temp ## class : LAScatalog (v1.2 format 2) ## extent : -20768836, 22184836, -17283836, 25668836 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) ## coord. ref. : NAD83(2011) / UTM zone 12N ## area : 57184906611 km² ## points : 5.24 billion points ## type : airborne ## density : 0 points/m² ## num. files : 187 that’s a lot of points…can an ordinary laptop handle it? we’ll find out. We’ll set the options in the function to generate a CHM which represents a DSM with the ground removed and no other filtering. This high resolution (i.e. fine-grain) CHM will serve as the foundation for tree detection and slash pile detection as we can manipulate it to optimize the processing for both methods. # outdir c2t_output_dir <- "../data" c2t_process_dir <- file.path(c2t_output_dir, "point_cloud_processing_delivery") c2t_tracking_fnm <- file.path(c2t_process_dir, "processed_tracking_data.csv") ############################################################## # cloud2trees::cloud2raster ############################################################## if( !file.exists( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "chm_0.1m.tif") ) || !file.exists( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "dtm_0.25m.tif") ) ){ # time it st_temp <- Sys.time() # run it # cloud2trees cloud2raster_ans <- cloud2trees::cloud2raster( output_dir = c2t_output_dir , input_las_dir = f , accuracy_level = 2 , keep_intrmdt = T , dtm_res_m = 0.25 , chm_res_m = 0.1 , min_height = 0 # effectively generates a DSM based on non-ground points ) # timer mins_temp <- difftime(Sys.time(),st_temp,units = "mins") %>% as.numeric() # save tracking dplyr::tibble( timer_cloud2raster_mins = mins_temp ) %>% write.csv( file = c2t_tracking_fnm , row.names = F, append = F ) }else{ dtm_temp <- terra::rast( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "dtm_0.25m.tif") ) chm_temp <- terra::rast( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "chm_0.1m.tif") ) cloud2raster_ans <- list( "dtm_rast" = dtm_temp , "chm_rast" = chm_temp ) } let’s see what we got from cloud2trees::cloud2raster() cloud2raster_ans %>% names() ## [1] "dtm_rast" "chm_rast" there’s a DTM # plot to check out the fine-resolution DTM raster cloud2raster_ans$dtm_rast %>% terra::plot(col = harrypotter::hp(n=100, option = "mischief"), main = "DTM (m)") there’s a CHM # plot to check out the fine-resolution CHM raster cloud2raster_ans$chm_rast %>% terra::plot(col = viridis::plasma(n=100), main = "CHM (m)") let’s see some details about the CHM # what chm? The local maximum filter algorithm allows for a constant window size or a variable window size defined by a function. See the lidR package book section by point cloud processing expert Jean-Romain Roussel for excellent detail on ITD and defining window size. The itd_tuning() function is used to visually assess tree crown delineation results from different window size functions used for the detection of individual trees. itd_tuning() allows users to test different window size functions on a sample of data to determine which function is most suitable for the area being analyzed. The preferred function can then be used in the ws parameter in raster2trees() and cloud2trees(). Section 4 Individual Tree Accuracy Evaluation In this section, we’ll mask the point cloud detected trees using the slash pile detections to get our final UAS point cloud-derived forest inventory tree list. Then we’ll bring in field-measured data to evaluate our tree detection accuracy. This accuracy evaluation will yield detection accuracy metric including precision, recall (i.e. detection rate), and F-score (overall accuracy or balanced accuracy). Precision is a measure of the proportion of trees that estimated by the UAS method that were actually trees. Recall is a measure of the proportion of field-measured trees that the UAS method correctly identified. The F-score balances precision and recall to create an overall accuracy measure. All of these metrics range between 0 and 1 with values close to one indicating higher tree detection accuracies. In open canopy ponderosa pine forests, tree detection rates generally range from 65-85% (Creasey et al. 2021; Swayze and Tinkham 2023; Tinkham and Woolsey 2024) with higher proportions of larger trees (e.g. 75-95%) being detected compared to smaller tree detection rates (55-75%). Field inventories carry well-documented challenges, including measurement error, subjective assessments, and data transcription errors (Elzinga et al. 2005; Westfall and Woodall 2007; Luoma et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2019; Sparks et al. 2024). This means that a comparison of the remote sensing forest measurement method against field data evaluates alignment with current operational practices rather than absolute environmental reality. Here are the notes I got along with the field inventory data: Attached is a csv of the PJ data from the Dawson Creek site. I added the plot center locations and calculated locations of each measured tree from the original distance and azimuth information. Below is a list of notes (and unfortunately some weird things) about it. There are 65 rows (out of 1603) with any missing data. The missing parts are usually in a location-related column with several in a tree metric column. There are 43 DRC (diameter at root collar) observations with two separate values separated by a comma. There are 8 circumstances where there are potential duplicate trees - where plot, distance, and azimuth are identical, but tree information is different. In the metadata crown length is described as “length from first longest side of the adult tree canopy, in m” and crown width is described as “width from second longest side of the adult tree canopy, in m”. However, crown width is frequently greater than the length value and after some looking the length value doesn’t seem to equal height-cbh either. The plot column includes unit, treatment type, and plot ID whereas the tree_id column includes that information as well as a per-plot ID of each tree. The multiple DRC values are due to multiple stems splitting at ground level. I think we should treat these as one tree, as they’re recorded in the data. To combine the two stem values into a single DRC, we could either take the larger of the two or sum them. The location duplication issue is due to two trees (or more likely stems from the same individual that split below ground) growing very close together. We should continue to treat them as separate trees, as shown in the data. Height, cbh, length and width are all in meters. DRC is in cm. Those crown and CBH measurements are suspect. we’ll also use the horizontal crown length and width to evaluate the UAS prediction of canopy cover on a plot-level basis. this canopy cover evaluation will: average the field measured horizontal crown length and width to approximate a circular diameter (Williams et al. 2020) use the diameter to calculate a 2D circular crown area for each field tree calculate the proportion of each plot covered by these assumed circular crowns for each plot, compare this proportion to the proportion of the plot predicted to be covered by crowns of UAS trees whose tree top point falls within the plot. requiring the tree top point to fall within the plot prior to calculating crown cover mimics the field technique of only measuring stems within a plot. the caveats attached to this approach are that it is notoriously difficult to measure crown dimensions using field techniques (source 2011) and the simple circular shape assumption does not match parameters to match predicted trees with validation/reference trees: pred_data: predicted data point locations as sf data ref_data: reference/validation/ground truth data point locations as sf data max_dist_m: radius of search for matching max_height_error_m: maximum allowable difference in height for to be considered correct match for work in ponderosa pine forests, we generally set the max_dist_m to a 3 m radius to account for tree lean and slight horizontal misalignment in GPS data collection with 3 m representing the crown radius of a mature tree. we also typically set the max_height_error_m to 2 m for ponderosa pine evaluation but will need to reduce here to account for shorter trees information used to inform the definition of “typical” crown width can be found in: Gill et al. 2000 Bechtold 2003 Bechtold 2004 Purves et al. 2007 Then, we’ll aggregate the instance matching results to evaluate omission rate (false negative rate or miss rate), commission rate (false positive rate), precision, recall (detection rate), and the F-score metric. As a reminder, true positive (TP) instances correctly match ground truth instances with a prediction, commission predictions do not match a ground truth instance (false positive; FP), and omissions are ground truth instances for which no predictions match (false negative; FN) \[\textrm{omission rate} = \frac{FN}{TP+FN}\] \[\textrm{commission rate} = \frac{FP}{TP+FP}\] \[\textrm{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\] \[\textrm{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\] \[ \textrm{F-score} = 2 \times \frac{\bigl(precision \times recall \bigr)}{\bigl(precision + recall \bigr)} \] ############################################################### ############################################################### ############################################################### ############################################################### # dplyr::case_when( dplyr::coalesce(precision,0) == 0 | dplyr::coalesce(recall,0) == 0 ~ 0 , T ~ 2 * ( (precision*recall)/(precision+recall) ) ) ) } all field plots 4.4 Physical Measurement Accuracy Overview Physical measurement accuracy metrics such as RMSE, MAPE, and Mean Error of tree form measurements (e.g. height, diameter) are calculated by aggregating the differences between the estimated tree attributes and the field reference values for instances classified as True Positives. These metrics tell us about the method’s ability to accurately quantify the form of the trees it successfully identified. to prepare our results for analysis, we will develop a function that aggregates the tree-level data into a single record for each metric-error measurement combination. this function will calculate detection performance metrics such as F-score, precision, and recall (using the confusion_matrix_scores_fn() we defined above), as well as physical measurement accuracy metrics including Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Error (ME), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) to assess the accuracy of our tree form measurements. this could be a valuable function for any future analysis comparing predictions to reference data. here are the physical measurement accuracy metric formulas: \[ \textrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_{i} - \hat{y_{i}})^{2}}{N}} \] \[ \textrm{ME} = \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\hat{y_{i}} - y_{i})}{N} \] \[ \textrm{MAPE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left| \frac{y_{i} - \hat{y_{i}}}{y_{i}} \right| \] Where \(N\) is equal to the total number of correctly matched trees, \(y_i\) is the ground truth measured value and \(\hat{y_i}\) is the predicted value of \(i\) There is a lot going on in our agg_ground_truth_match() function but it’s application is straightforward enough: The minimum required input is a data frame of the raw instance matches with a column named match_grp which is string/factor with the levels “true positive”, “commission”, and “omission” as returned by the ground_truth_prediction_match() function Optionally, if the data contain columns with the prefix “diff_” the mean error (ME) is calculated for those columns with the return having the suffix “_mean” and the RMSE is calculated for those columns with the return having the suffix “_rmse” interpretation of the ME is enhanced if these “diff_” columns are calculated as the predicted value minus the actual value (e.g. pred_diameter_m - gt_diameter_m) Optionally, if the data contain columns with the prefix “pct_diff_” the mean absolute percent error (MAPE) is calculated for those columns with the return having the suffix “_mape” these “pct_diff_” columns are calculated as the actual value minus the predicted value divided by the actual value (e.g. (gt_diameter_m - pred_diameter_m)/gt_diameter_m) 4.4.1 Example: Physical Traditional silvicultural metrics like basal area and volume are not particularly useful for managing these woodlands because the trees/shrubs feature highly irregular, multi-stemmed growth forms. Furthermore, field inventories like FIA measure diameter at root collar (DRC) instead of standard diameter at breast height (DBH) and then convert those metrics using regional allometric equations. Because of this, it is probably inappropriate for us to quantify the accuracy of UAS-predicted DBH, which is modeled using a height-to-DBH equation from local FIA data, against field-calculated DBH values derived from converted DRC measurements. Instead, modern management evaluations in these pinyon-juniper systems prioritize tree density measurements and canopy clump configurations to analyze structural and spatial patterns. This focus on horizontal canopy architecture, tracking trees per hectare and interspace connectivity, provides a much more direct and ecologically meaningful way to evaluate ecosystem health and fire risk across these arid landscapes. 4.9 Canopy Cover Evaluation Let’s shift our focus to evaluating UAS-predicted canopy cover compared to field-measured values. Recall that to obtain field-measured canopy cover, we averaged the field-recorded horizontal crown length and width to approximate a circular diameter, used that diameter to calculate a 2D circular crown area for each tree, and determined the proportion of each plot covered by these assumed circular crowns. For each plot, we’ll compare this proportion to the canopy cover predicted by the UAS using trees whose tree-top points fall within the plot boundaries irrespective of if a tree was matched as a true positive in our instance matching evaluation. Requiring the tree-top point to fall within the plot mimics the field technique of only measuring stems located inside the plot boundaries. The main caveats attached to this canopy cover accuracy evaluation are that measuring crown dimensions accurately using manual ground techniques is notoriously difficult, and the simple circular shape assumption rarely matches the irregular crown morphologies found in the real-world (Rautiainen et al. 2008; Gallardo-Salazar & Pompa-García 2020; Ren et al. 2024). # The UAS approach delineates crowns from an aerial perspective and utilizes a segmentation routine that prevents any two crowns from overlapping. Conversely, the field method assumes a perfectly circular crown extending symmetrically from the tree stem. In dense stands, this circular geometry causes field-calculated crowns to overlap in 2D space which may artificially reduce the total canopy cover. In reality, tree branches grow asymmetrically. For example, extending away from competitors to capture available sunlight. The UAS captures this irregular, outward branch expansion which may explain why it results in larger (and more realistic) canopy cover measurements than the field-based method. let’s check out a visual representation of that phenomenon by looking as some example plots # We can move beyond summary canopy cover percentages and evaluate the spatial overlap of the crown footprints using the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric. The IoU index provides a spatial assessment by measuring the geographic alignment between the UAS crown polygons and circular field crowns. To quantify the spatial agreement between your UAS-delineated crowns and the field-calculated circular crowns, IoU is calculated by dividing the area of overlap between the two crown layers by the total combined area of both layers: \[ \text{IoU}=\frac{\text{Area of Intersection}}{\text{Area of Union}}=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|} \] where \(A\) represents the spatial footprint of the field-calculated circular crowns within a plot and \(B\) represents the spatial footprint of the UAS-segmented crown polygons within the same plot. # Section 6 Tree Group Analysis 6.1 Group Tree Crowns 6.2 Identify Openings 6.3 Tree Clump Summary 6.4 Openings Summary 6.5 Treatment Compliance Evaluation

Section 6 Tree Group Analysis Evaluate the spatial configuration of the detected trees focusing on horizontal heterogeneity and an investigation of tree clumps and openings. some relevant work includes: Spatial Patterns of Pinyon–Juniper Woodland Expansion in Central Nevada (Weisberg et al. 2007) Density-dependent tree mortality in pinyon-juniper woodlands (Greenwood and Weisberg 2008) Long-Term Effectiveness of Tree Removal to Re-Establish Sagebrush Steppe Vegetation and Associated Spatial Patterns in Surface Conditions and Soil Hydrologic Properties (Williams et al. 2020) 6.1 Group Tree Crowns While some research on tree spatial patterns use tree point locations buffered with a fixed radius (e.g. 3 m) to approximate the crown radius of a “typical” overstory tree (e.g. Churchill et al. (2016)), we’ll use the irregular, more realistic crown shapes identified from the aerial data to determine tree clump groups. Remember we are only looking at what could be considered “overstory” trees since we filtered the tree list to keep only trees that meet a certain minimum height threshold of 2 m treetops_sf %>% sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::select(tree_height_m) %>% summary() %>% knitr::kable(format = "markdown") tree_height_m Min. : 2.00 1st Qu.: 3.52 Median : 4.59 Mean : 4.60 3rd Qu.: 5.58 Max. :18.76 Since a primary objective of this analysis is to evaluate how different treatments influence forest structure, we’ll treat each unit as a discrete area and exclude any trees located outside of the unit boundaries from the clump classification process. This approach assumes that trees within a unit do not form functional clusters with those in adjacent areas (even though some units share a common border and we have data extending beyond the unit boundaries). This assumption prevents data from untreated control areas or differently treated areas from influencing the results when summarized by treatment type. This intentional ignorance of edge effects means that the scale of focus of this analysis is strictly on the treatment unit. define a function to make the tree clump groupings by treatment unit get_clumps_temp <- function(tree_list, buffer = 0) { # buffer and dissolve (arcGIS logic) clump_polys <- tree_list %>% dplyr::ungroup() %>% sf::st_buffer(buffer) %>% sf::st_union() %>% sf::st_cast("POLYGON") %>% sf::st_as_sf() %>% dplyr::mutate(clump_id = dplyr::row_number()) # We’ll identify openings based on their distance from the nearest tree crown. We’ll use this same 1 m distance threshold in defining treeless openings, where each opening will be required to comprise continuous space at least 1 m away from the nearest tree. This 1 m buffer accounts for the zone of immediate canopy influence and ensures that areas categorized as open are functionally distinct from the canopy. This threshold is flexible and can be adjusted to meet specific management or analysis objectives (e.g. flame length; wildlife corridors). First, we’ll generate a distance raster where each cell represents the distance to the nearest tree clump group (i.e. crown) within the treatment unit boundary. Areas with a distance value of 1 m or greater are classified as openings and are defined by spatial connectedness, not a specific geometric shape. As such, they may be irregularly shaped as they are allowed to wind between clumps to follow a path where trees are distant. A single opening continues as long as the flow of open space is not entirely obstructed by surrounding tree groups. Once a gap is completely surrounded by canopy, the opening is closed off and is treated as a discrete spatial feature. # create function to pass a return from get_clump_summary() and get a distance raster get_clump_dist_rast_temp <- function(x, clump_dist_m = 3){ # For this specific project, the “uniform” thinning treatments provided explicit instructions for the spatial arrangement of post-treatment stand conditions: Uniform - Low Light intensity thinning: Leave 15 feet between tree crowns. 70% of the retained (i.e. leave) trees should be over 8 inches basal diameter if present and 30% should be between 2 inches and 8 inches in basal diameter. Uniform - High Heavy intensity thinning: Leave at least 30 feet between tree crowns; 70% of the retained (i.e. leave) trees should be over 8 inches basal diameter if present and 30% should be between 2 inches and 8 inches in basal diameter. The following is a subset of items provided in the general guidance for both “uniform” prescriptions that are most relevant for our evaluation: Cut all dead pinyon trees <8 inches in basal diameter. Leave all other standing dead trees for wildlife snags. Dead trees are not considered when applying the spacing guides above. Remove 70% of all woody shrubs (i.e. gambel oak and serviceberry); retain all gambel oak stems greater than 3 inches in basal diameter. All trees with green spray paint should be not be cut and piles should be placed at least 15 ft from the canopy of those trees. These have a small piece of equipment that are recording tree growth (Fig. 2). These point dendrometers are on the bole (main stem) of the tree, located 1-2 feet above the ground on the east side of the tree, and a shapefile of the trees approximate location has been provided. In addition to the above, the following apply: …. Except for leave trees, all live trees having a minimum size of one (1) inch basal diameter and a height of 12 inches shall be cut. Retain trees that contain raptor nests. No ponderosa pine trees should be cut Since we know our UAS-based individual tree delineation does not perfectly align with field-marked trees (62% F-score), we’ll combine UAS-delineated tree crowns that are spatially continuous (i.e. directly touching or overlapping) into singular “tree objects” for this evaluation of the treatment tree spacing compliance. We’ll then calculate the distance between spatially distinct post treatment tree objects for comparison against the prescription targets. Additionally, since the prescription requires that priority trees like ponderosa pine and wildlife trees are not removed, and thus excluded from the spacing guidelines, the average space between residual trees should be slightly lower than the targets (even if the spacing is perfectly implemented to prescription) due to these restrictions which require keeping more trees than would be needed to meet the spacing guidelines. As a reminder, we are only evaluating UAS-detected tree objects that have a minimum height of 2 m and have a top point that falls within a treatment unit boundary. This approach assumes that trees within a unit do not form functional clusters with those in adjacent areas (even though some units share a common border and we have data extending beyond the unit boundaries). This assumption prevents data from untreated control areas or differently treated areas from influencing the results when summarized by treatment type. This intentional ignorance of edge effects means that the scale of focus of this analysis is strictly on the treatment unit.
